questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to train a dog to use a toilet
The history of London's sewers and rivers
Whether humans are naturally clean
Why cats are better pets than dogs
questions.why: Neil says they'll ask whether humans as a species are naturally clean and tidy.

questions.q: What does Sam say about how humans deal with waste?
options: Humans have always been much cleaner than animals
Humans often deal with waste badly
Humans only make waste in cities
Humans learned it from cats
questions.why: Sam says from dumping raw sewage into rivers to littering, humans aren't always good with waste.

questions.q: What do leaf-cutter ants do, according to Neil?
options: They bury their waste in deep holes far from the nest
They clean the bodies of other, larger animals
They leave their waste in piles near their home
They kill dirty ants trying to come back into the group
questions.why: Neil says leaf-cutter ants kill any dirty ants trying to re-enter the group.

questions.q: According to Professor Adam Hart, why do some antelope use a special area for their waste?
options: To mark their territory for other animals
To keep their babies safe from disease
To stop humans from finding them
Because they don't like the smell
questions.why: He says animals often use dung and urine as territorial markers to say 'this is my territory'.

questions.q: According to Dr Michael De Barra, what is human cleanliness linked to?
options: Living close together in big, crowded cities
Religious beliefs and old traditions
The problem of infectious diseases
Copying the behaviour of other animals
questions.why: Sam says he thinks human attitudes to cleanliness are related to the problem of infectious diseases.

questions.q: What kinds of things cause disgust, according to Dr De Barra?
options: Only food that has gone bad
Bright colours and loud noises
Things we have never seen before
Possible signs of disease
questions.why: He says it's triggered by infectious disease threats like smells, body wastes, coughs and sneezes.

questions.q: What is the purpose of feelings like disgust and nausea, according to the presenters?
options: They warn us away from sources of illness
They help us digest our food more quickly
They show that we are already ill
They make us want to clean our homes
questions.why: Sam says they are the immune system's way of saying 'keep away! – this will make you sick!'

questions.q: How does Sam feel near the end of the programme?
options: Hungry and ready for her lunch
Disgusted by the talk of pee and poo
Bored by all the science and facts
Proud of how clean humans are
questions.why: Sam says, 'All this talk of pee and poo is disgusting!'
